| Edges | `Edges` | Multi-button | 0: Black (1: Wrap, 2: Duplicate) | How the image is sampled outside the frame. |

**See also:** Relative Transform (Krokodove), Segment Transform (Krokodove), Stretch (Krokodove), Mirror (Krokodove).

## rCube (`KD_Region3DCube`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Region · **Short name:** rCub · **Inputs:** none · **Output:** `Output` (Region)

Creates a box-shaped region. Inside the box a point of a 3D scene counts as fully in the region, outside it does not, and Softness feathers the faces. A region isn't rendered: it is passed to a 3D Krokodove tool, such as Kill3D, that uses it to decide where its effect applies. See the Krokodove: Region overview for how regions are built and used.

**Use for:** limiting a 3D effect to a box-shaped volume, such as the particles or objects inside a title's bounding area.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Invert | `Invert` | Checkbox | 0 | Swaps inside and outside. |
| Softness Lock | `SoftnessLock` | Checkbox | 1 | Keeps the three softness values equal, so setting X sets all of them. |
| Softness X, Y, Z | `SoftnessX`, `SoftnessY`, `SoftnessZ` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Width of the feather on each pair of faces. 0 gives hard edges. |
| Transform | `TransformPositionX`, `TransformPositionY`, `TransformPositionZ`, `TransformRotationOrder`, `TransformRotationX`, `TransformRotationY`, `TransformRotationZ`, `TransformScaleLock`, `TransformScaleX`, `TransformScaleY`, `TransformScaleZ` | Number | see Common Controls → Krokodove tools | Moves, rotates and scales the box. At default size the box runs from −1 to 1 on each axis. |

**See also:** rSphere, rPlane, rMerge, rModify, rTransform, Krokodove: Region overview.

## rMerge (`KD_Region3DMerge`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Region · **Short name:** rMrg · **Inputs:** `Region1` (Region), `Region2` (Region) · **Output:** `Output` (Region)

Combines two regions into one with a set operation: union, intersection, add, subtract or exclusive. It is how you build a region out of several shapes, such as a box with a sphere cut out of it. Region 2 is optional, and an unconnected Region 2 counts as empty. Each input can itself be the output of another region tool, so merges can be chained.

**Use for:** joining primitive regions into one volume, and cutting one volume out of another.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Region 1, Region 2 | `Region1`, `Region2` | Region input | none | The two regions to combine. |
| Combine | `Combine` | Multi-button | 0 (0: Union, 1: Intersect, 2: Add, 3: Subtract, 4: Exclusive) | The operation. Union covers either region, Intersect only where both are, Subtract removes Region 2 from Region 1, and Exclusive covers each region but not their overlap. |
| Invert | `Invert` | Checkbox | 0 | Swaps inside and outside after the combination. |

**See also:** rCube, rSphere, rModify, rTransform, Krokodove: Region overview.

## rModify (`KD_Region3DModify`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Region · **Short name:** rMod · **Inputs:** `Region` (Region) · **Output:** `Output` (Region)

Adjusts the values of a region: how bright (how far inside), how contrasted (how hard the edge) and whether only its soft edge is kept. Brightness and Contrast change how much of the region counts as inside. Edge only keeps the transition at the boundary and drops the solid interior, which turns a volume into a shell. The Use Shape and Shape controls are present in the tool but have no effect in the current source.

**Use for:** making a region tighter or softer, and using only the edge of a volume so that a 3D effect hits the surface of an area.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Region | `Region` | Region input | none | The region to modify. |
| Invert | `Invert` | Checkbox | 0 | Swaps inside and outside. |
| Brightness | `Brightness` | Number | 0 (−1 to 1) | Shifts the values, so the region covers more or less. |
| Contrast | `Contrast` | Number | 1 (0–5) | Spreads the values around the middle. Higher values give harder edges. |
| Edge only | `Edgeonly` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Blends towards the boundary only: at 1 the interior of the region drops out and the edge remains. |
| Use Shape, Shape | `UseShape`, `Shape` | Checkbox, Spline | 0, none | Not documented. The current source doesn't apply them, so they have no effect. |

**See also:** rMerge, rTransform, rNoise, Krokodove: Region overview.

## rNoise (`KD_Region3DNoise`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Region · **Short name:** rNoi · **Inputs:** none · **Output:** `Output` (Region)

Creates a region from 3D noise. Each point in the scene gets a value between 0 and 1 from a smooth noise field, so the region is patchy and gradual rather than a clear inside and outside. Brightness and Contrast reshape the values. The noise seed is fixed, so the pattern is the same every time. Use Transform to move or scale the noise field, and animate its position to make the patches drift.

**Use for:** irregular, organic areas that limit a 3D effect, such as patchy zones where particles or objects are affected.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Invert | `Invert` | Checkbox | 0 | Swaps high and low values. |
| Brightness | `Brightness` | Number | 0 (−1 to 1) | Adds to every value, so the region covers more or less of the noise field. |
| Contrast | `Contrast` | Number | 1 (0–5) | Spreads the values around the middle. Higher values make the region more solid and the edges sharper. |
| Transform | `TransformPositionX`, `TransformPositionY`, `TransformPositionZ`, `TransformRotationOrder`, `TransformRotationX`, `TransformRotationY`, `TransformRotationZ`, `TransformScaleLock`, `TransformScaleX`, `TransformScaleY`, `TransformScaleZ` | Number | see Common Controls → Krokodove tools | Moves, rotates and scales the noise. Scale sets the size of the patches. |

**See also:** rCube, rSphere, rModify, Krokodove: Region overview.

## rPlane (`KD_Region3DPlane`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Region · **Short name:** rPla · **Inputs:** none · **Output:** `Output` (Region)

Creates a half-space: everything on one side of a plane is in the region, and everything on the other side is not. The side that counts is the one the plane's +Z direction points to, so rotating the plane turns the region. Only Softness Z changes the result, and it sets the width of the soft transition at the plane. The plane is not rendered; a 3D Krokodove tool uses it to limit its effect.

**Use for:** limiting an effect to everything above or below a horizon or a floor, and wiping a 3D effect across a scene.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Invert | `Invert` | Checkbox | 0 | Swaps the two sides of the plane. |
| Softness Lock | `SoftnessLock` | Checkbox | 1 | Keeps the softness values equal. |
| Softness Z | `SoftnessZ` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Width of the soft transition at the plane. 0 gives a hard edge. Softness X and Y are not used by the plane. |
| Transform | `TransformPositionX`, `TransformPositionY`, `TransformPositionZ`, `TransformRotationOrder`, `TransformRotationX`, `TransformRotationY`, `TransformRotationZ`, `TransformScaleLock`, `TransformScaleX`, `TransformScaleY`, `TransformScaleZ` | Number | see Common Controls → Krokodove tools | Moves and rotates the plane. Animate Position Z or Rotation to sweep it through a scene. |

**See also:** rCube, rSphere, rTransform, rMerge, Krokodove: Region overview.

## rSphere (`KD_Region3DSphere`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Region · **Short name:** rSph · **Inputs:** none · **Output:** `Output` (Region)

Creates a spherical region. Points inside the sphere count as fully in the region, and points outside do not. Only Softness X changes the result: it sets the width of the soft edge around the sphere. The sphere is not rendered; a 3D Krokodove tool uses it to limit its effect. See the Krokodove: Region overview.

**Use for:** a round volume that limits a 3D effect, such as a spherical area where objects are affected.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Invert | `Invert` | Checkbox | 0 | Swaps inside and outside. |
| Softness Lock | `SoftnessLock` | Checkbox | 1 | Keeps the softness values equal. |
| Softness X | `SoftnessX` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Width of the soft edge around the sphere. 0 gives a hard edge. The sphere's radius is 1 at default scale. |
| Transform | `TransformPositionX`, `TransformPositionY`, `TransformPositionZ`, `TransformRotationOrder`, `TransformRotationX`, `TransformRotationY`, `TransformRotationZ`, `TransformScaleLock`, `TransformScaleX`, `TransformScaleY`, `TransformScaleZ` | Number | see Common Controls → Krokodove tools | Moves, rotates and scales the sphere. Scale sets its radius. |

Softness Y and Softness Z are not used by the sphere.

**See also:** rCube, rPlane, rMerge, Krokodove: Region overview.

## rTransform (`KD_Region3DTransform`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Region · **Short name:** rXf · **Inputs:** `Region` (Region) · **Output:** `Output` (Region)

Moves, rotates and scales an existing region without changing its shape. It works like a null for a region: connect the region to Region, then set the Transform controls. Chain it after rMerge or rModify to position a combined volume, or animate it to make a region travel through a scene.

**Use for:** moving a region along a path, turning a box or plane, and scaling a region up or down.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Region | `Region` | Region input | none | The region to transform. |
| Invert | `Invert` | Checkbox | 0 | Swaps inside and outside. |
| Transform | `TransformPositionX`, `TransformPositionY`, `TransformPositionZ`, `TransformRotationOrder`, `TransformRotationX`, `TransformRotationY`, `TransformRotationZ`, `TransformScaleLock`, `TransformScaleX`, `TransformScaleY`, `TransformScaleZ` | Number | see Common Controls → Krokodove tools | Position, rotation and scale of the region. |

**See also:** rMerge, rModify, rCube, rPlane, Krokodove: Region overview.

## sExtrude (`KD_ShapeExtrude`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape · **Short name:** sExtr · **Inputs:** `Input` (ShapeTree, required) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Gives a shape depth by sweeping its outline along a direction and joining the copy to the original, the way a solid is extruded. Angle sets the direction of the depth, and Length sets how far it goes.

**Use for:** drop shadows with depth, 3D-looking type and logos built from flat shapes, and extruded outlines in a motion title.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Angle | `Angle` | Number | −45 (0–360, degrees) | Direction of the depth. |
| Length | `Length` | Number | 0.05 (0–0.2) | How far the extrusion goes, in shape units. |

**See also:** sOffset, sExpand, sRender, sWriteOn, sTransform.

## sKill (`KD_ShapeKill`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape · **Short name:** sKil · **Inputs:** `Input` (ShapeTree, required) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Cuts a shape's path into pieces by removing the segments that fail a test. Segments are tested by their direction (By Angle) and by their length (By Length). A segment that passes is kept, and one that fails is removed, which leaves gaps in the path. Note the name: a segment is killed when it doesn't match the range. The default Angle range of 0 to 90 degrees keeps only the segments whose direction lies in the first quarter turn.

**Use for:** breaking an outline into dashes or partial pieces, and keeping only the parts of a path that run in one direction or are of one length.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| By Angle | `ByAngle` | Checkbox | 1 | Tests each segment's direction against the Angle range. |
| Angle Minimum, Angle Maximum | `AngleMinimum`, `AngleMaximum` | Number | 0, 90 (0–360, degrees) | The directions that are kept. The range wraps past 360 degrees if the minimum is greater than the maximum. |
| Angle Offset | `AngleOffset` | Number | 0 (0–360, degrees) | Turns the Angle range, so the kept directions can be rotated without changing the range. |
| By Length | `ByLength` | Checkbox | 0 | Tests each segment's length against the Length range. |
| Length Minimum, Length Maximum | `LengthMinimum`, `LengthMaximum` | Number | 0, 0.1 (0–0.5) | The segment lengths that are kept, in shape units. |

When both tests are on, a segment must pass both to be kept.

**See also:** sResample, sWriteOn, sZigZag, sRender.

## sOffset (`KD_ShapeOffset`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape · **Short name:** sOff · **Inputs:** `Input` (ShapeTree, required) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Makes copies of a shape's outline at steps away from it, so each copy is a ring or echo around the original. Offset sets the distance of each step, Number sets how many steps are made, and Sides chooses whether the rings grow outwards, shrink inwards or go both ways. Offset Join Type sets how the corners of each ring are joined. The result is a set of outlines that keep the input's style, so it works well with write-on, stroke colour changes and staggered animation.

**Use for:** concentric outline rings and ripples, echo or glow strokes, and a border around a shape at a set distance.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Keep Original | `KeepOriginal` | Checkbox | 0 | Adds the input shape to the output, unchanged, alongside the offset copies. |
| Number | `Number` | Number | 1 (1–16) | How many copies are made on each side. |
| Offset | `Offset` | Number | 0.01 (−0.1 to 0.1) | Distance between successive copies, in shape units. The copies are at 1×, 2×, … this distance from the input. |
| Offset Join Type | `OffsetJoinType` | Multi-button | 0 (0: Miter, 1: Bevel, 2: Rounded) | How corners are joined on each copy. Rounded gives smooth corners; Miter gives sharp points that can extend far at acute angles. |
| Sides | `Sides` | Multi-button | 2 (0: Both, 1: Inside, 2: Outside) | Which way the copies go. Outside grows the shape, Inside shrinks it, and Both makes copies on each side. |

### Example

Three outward rings around a rounded rectangle, staggered in time with Keep Original off, rendered and merged over the video:

```python
rect = comp.AddTool('sRectangle')
rect.Solid = 0
rect.Width = 0.3
rect.Height = 0.2
rect.CornerRadius = 0.3

rings = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapeOffset')
rings.Input = rect.Output
rings.Number = 3
rings.Offset = 0.02
rings.Sides = 2                         # Outside
rings.OffsetJoinType = 2                # Rounded

render = comp.AddTool('sRender')
render.Input = rings.Output

merge = comp.AddTool('Merge')
merge.Background = media_in.Output
merge.Foreground = render.Output
```

### Tips

- Animate Offset from 0 upwards to make rings expand outwards from the shape. Keep Number and Sides fixed.
- With Sides set to Inside, the copies shrink into the shape. Negative Offset values also reverse the direction.
- Use Rounded join for soft glow-like rings. Use Miter for sharp, graphic outlines, and Bevel for a neutral look.
- To give the rings their own colour and line settings, follow sOffset with sRestyle.

**See also:** sExpand, sOutline, sRound, sRestyle, sWriteOn, sRender.

## sResample (`KD_ShapeResample`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape · **Short name:** sRes · **Inputs:** `Input` (ShapeTree, required) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Re-spaces the points along a shape's path, placing a new point every Distance along the outline. The shape keeps its line but its points are evenly spaced, which is what tools that work point by point, such as sZigZag, need. Offset slides the starting point along the path, and the end points can be kept as they are.

**Use for:** evenly spaced points before a zigzag, and resetting a path made of uneven segments.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Distance | `Distance` | Number | 0.11 (0.0001–1) | Spacing between the new points, in shape units. Smaller values give more points. |
| Offset | `Offset` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Slides where the first point falls along the path, in the same units as Distance. |
| Keep End Points | `KeepEndPoints` | Checkbox | 0 | Keeps the path's first and last points, so the ends don't move. |
| Keep Original Points | `KeepOriginalPoints` | Checkbox | 0 | Keeps the existing points, in addition to the new ones. |
| Minimum Angle | `MinimumAngle` | Number | 20 (0–360, degrees) | Not documented. The value is set but the source doesn't use it, so it has no effect. |
| Curve Precision | `CurvePrecision` | Number | 8 (2–16) | How finely curves are flattened into straight pieces before the points are placed. |

**See also:** sZigZag, sSmooth, sRound, sKill.

## sRestyle (`KD_ShapeRestyle`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape · **Short name:** sRSt · **Inputs:** `Input` (ShapeTree, required) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Gives every shape in the input a new style, from this tool's Style tab. Type decides what happens to the old style: Replace clears it and applies the new one, while Add keeps the existing fill and outline and adds this tool's on top. Nothing changes unless this tool's fill or outline is turned on in its Style tab.

**Use for:** recolouring a group of shapes from one node, and adding an outline to shapes that have a fill.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Type | `Type` | Combo | 0 (0: Replace, 1: Add) | Replace removes the input's style and applies this tool's. Add appends this tool's fill and outline to the input's style. |

The Style tab (fill, outline, opacity, line options) is shared with the other styled Krokodove shape tools; see Common Controls → Krokodove tools.

**See also:** sChangeStyle, sOffset, sRender.

## sRound (`KD_ShapeRound`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape · **Short name:** sRnd · **Inputs:** `Input` (ShapeTree, required) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Rounds the corners of a shape's path. Each sharp corner is replaced by a curve of the given Radius, and the Angle Minimum and Angle Maximum range decides which corners are rounded: corners that are nearly straight, or nearly folded back on themselves, are left alone. The radius is always limited to half of the adjoining segment, so neighbouring corners never overlap. Use it on a polygon, a star or a rectangle outline to soften it, or to get rounded corners on a shape that has none.

**Use for:** soft-cornered boxes, rounded star and polygon shapes, and rounded outlines for write-on.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Radius | `Radius` | Number | 0.01 (0–0.05) | Size of the rounding, in shape units. Larger values round more of each corner. |
| Symmetrical | `Symmetrical` | Checkbox | 1 | On: both sides of a corner use the smaller of the two possible radii, so the curve stays balanced. Off: each side uses its own limit, which can make the curve lopsided. |
| Tension | `Tension` | Number | 0.5 (0–1) | Length of the curve's handles. Higher values give a rounder, more gradual bend. |
| Angle | `Angle` | Number | 0 (−180 to 180) | Turns the rounding handles about the corner. Not documented; the effect is only checked in the source. |
| Angle Minimum, Angle Maximum | `AngleMinimum`, `AngleMaximum` | Number | 20, 160 (10–170, degrees) | The corners that get rounded. A corner is rounded when its turn, measured from a straight line, lies between these values. |

### Example

A star with rounded points, rendered and merged over the video:

```python
star = comp.AddTool('sStar')
star.Points = 5

rnd = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapeRound')
rnd.Input = star.Output
rnd.Radius = 0.03
rnd.Tension = 0.6
rnd.AngleMinimum = 30
rnd.AngleMaximum = 170

render = comp.AddTool('sRender')
render.Input = rnd.Output

merge = comp.AddTool('Merge')
merge.Background = media_in.Output
merge.Foreground = render.Output
```

### Tips

- If a corner doesn't round, check the Angle range first. Very sharp corners (near 180 degrees of turn) sit above Angle Maximum, and near-straight points sit below Angle Minimum.
- Radius is capped by the length of the adjoining edges. On a shape with short edges, a large Radius rounds less than you asked for, so use a smaller Radius or a larger shape.
- To round only the corners of a rectangle, leave the range at its default: the four 90-degree corners are inside it.
- Animate Radius for a shape that morphs from square to round. Animate `AngleMinimum` to exclude some corners.

**See also:** sSmooth, sZigZag, sResample, sRectangle, sStar, sRender.

## sSmooth (`KD_ShapeSmooth`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape · **Short name:** sSmo · **Inputs:** `Input` (ShapeTree, required) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Turns the straight segments of a path into smooth curves that pass through the same points. Smooth sets how curved the result is, from straight lines at 0 to full smoothing at 1, and Smooth Curvature sets how strongly each curve bends through its neighbouring points. The points themselves don't move.

**Use for:** smoothing a hand-placed or traced outline, turning a polygon into a blob or organic shape, and softening a zigzag or star after it has been created.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Smooth | `Smooth` | Number | 1 (0–1) | 0 leaves the path as straight lines between points. 1 gives full smoothing. |
| Smooth Curvature | `SmoothCurvature` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Scales how far each curve bends towards its neighbouring points. At 0 the path stays straight, whatever Smooth is set to. Higher values bend it more. |

### Example

A trace-like polygon smoothed into a blob, rendered and merged over the video:

```python
poly = comp.AddTool('sNGon')
poly.Sides = 6
poly.Solid = 0

smooth = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapeSmooth')
smooth.Input = poly.Output
smooth.Smooth = 0.8
smooth.SmoothCurvature = 1.0

render = comp.AddTool('sRender')
render.Input = smooth.Output

merge = comp.AddTool('Merge')
merge.Background = media_in.Output
merge.Foreground = render.Output
```

### Tips

- Animate Smooth from 0 to 1 to morph a polygon into a rounded, organic outline. Set it back to 0 to return the straight edges.
- Smooth needs at least three points. A two-point line passes through unchanged.
- Smooth keeps the points, so a shape with few points stays close to its original outline. Add points first with sResample if you need more control.
- Use sRound instead when you want corners rounded but the straight edges kept.

**See also:** sRound, sZigZag, sResample, sNGon, sPolygon, sBSpline, sRender.

## sTriangulate (`KD_ShapeTriangulate`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape · **Short name:** sTri · **Inputs:** `Input` (ShapeTree, required) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Splits a filled shape into triangles, which fills it with a mesh of flat triangles. The result has the same outline as the input.

**Use for:** triangle or faceted graphics, and preparing a shape for tools that need flat faces.

It has no visible controls. The Type control is hidden in the Inspector. Its first option (the default) does the triangulation. The second option, Type 2, produces an empty shape, so leave Type at its default.

**See also:** sSmooth, sRound, sResample, sRender.

## sWriteOn (`KD_ShapeWriteOn`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape · **Short name:** sWri · **Inputs:** `Input` (ShapeTree, required) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Draws shape outlines on, or off, by showing only part of each outline's length. A range along the path, set by Range Start and Range End (0 is the start of the path, 1 its end), decides what is visible. Animate the range to write a shape on, or animate Shift to move a visible piece along the path. sWriteOn takes any shape tree, so it works on the results of other shape tools as well as on core shapes. Core shapes such as sRectangle also have their own write-on controls, but those only act on their own outline. The output still has to go through sRender.

**Use for:** write-on titles, logos and icons; drawing a path on; a travelling highlight or comet along an outline, using Shift.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Level | `Level` | Multi-button | 1: Shape. 0: Global, 1: Shape, 2: Element | Global treats the whole shape tree as one path, so a single animation writes its shapes on one after another. Shape and Element apply the range to each shape on its own. |
| Range Start, Range End | `RangeStart`, `RangeEnd` | Number | 0, 1 (0–1) | The visible part of each outline, as a fraction of its length. Animate `RangeEnd` from 0 to 1 to write on. |
| Shift | `Shift` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Moves the range along the outline, as a fraction of its length. Animate it for a moving highlight. |
| Shift Wrap | `ShiftWrap` | Checkbox | 1 | When the range runs past the end of the outline, the rest of it continues from the start, so the visible piece stays whole. |

### Example

A rectangle outline that writes on over 36 frames, rendered and merged over the video:

```python
rect = comp.AddTool('sRectangle')
rect.Solid = 0                          # outline only
rect.Width = 0.4
rect.Height = 0.2
rect.BorderWidth = 0.004

write = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapeWriteOn')
write.Input = rect.Output
write.RangeEnd = comp.BezierSpline()
write.RangeEnd[0] = 0.0                 # nothing drawn at frame 0
write.RangeEnd[36] = 1.0                # fully drawn at frame 36

render = comp.AddTool('sRender')
render.Input = write.Output

merge = comp.AddTool('Merge')
merge.Background = media_in.Output
merge.Foreground = render.Output
```

### Tips

- Set `Level` to Global to write a whole group of shapes in sequence from one `RangeEnd` animation. With Shape, each shape writes on at the same time.
- A moving highlight: keep `RangeStart` at 0 and `RangeEnd` at about 0.15, then animate `Shift` from 0 to 1 with Shift Wrap on.
- Write-on works on outlines. A filled shape has no path to draw along, so set Solid to 0 on sRectangle or sEllipse first, or give the outline a border with sOutline.

**See also:** sZigZag, sRound, sResample, sRender, sRectangle (its own WriteLength), sPolygon, sBSpline.

## sZigZag (`KD_ShapeZigZag`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape · **Short name:** sZZ · **Inputs:** `Input` (ShapeTree, required) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Turns each straight segment of a shape's path into a zigzag, alternating the points to either side of the line. Steps sets how many teeth each segment gets, and Offset sets how far they stand out and to which side. Apply it to outlines to make hand-drawn, torn or electric-looking edges, or to a line that will be written on or duplicated.

**Use for:** scribbled or sketched outlines, torn-paper and lightning edges, and zigzag underlines or dividers.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Steps | `Steps` | Number | 3 (1–10) | Points per segment. Each step adds one zig or zag, so higher values make finer, more frequent teeth. |
| Offset | `Offset` | Number | 0.01 (−0.1 to 0.1) | How far the zigs stand out from the line, in shape units. The sign sets the side: a negative value starts on the other side. |

The Type ("By segment" or "By distance") and Distance controls exist, but they're hidden in the Inspector. Keep Type at 0 (By segment): By distance is not implemented, and the shape passes through unchanged.

### Example

A rectangle outline with a zigzag edge, rendered and merged over the video:

```python
rect = comp.AddTool('sRectangle')
rect.Solid = 0
rect.Width = 0.5
rect.Height = 0.3
rect.BorderWidth = 0.003

zig = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapeZigZag')
zig.Input = rect.Output
zig.Steps = 6
zig.Offset = 0.015

render = comp.AddTool('sRender')
render.Input = zig.Output

merge = comp.AddTool('Merge')
merge.Background = media_in.Output
merge.Foreground = render.Output
```

### Tips

- Steps and Offset are the two controls to animate. Animating Offset from positive to negative makes the teeth flicker between sides.
- Put sZigZag before sWriteOn to write a zigzag line on.
- The zigzag is a fixed pattern. For random variation, put sJitter from the core shape tools after it.

**See also:** sWriteOn, sSmooth, sRound, sOffset, sRender, sJitter, sOutline.

## sPrimitive Create (`KD_ShapePrimitiveCreate`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape Create · **Short name:** sPriC · **Inputs:** none · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Generates a basic shape: a cross, a regular polygon, a rectangle or a star. Choose the shape with Type, then set its overall size with Size X and Size Y, and its number of sides or points with Steps. Like every shape generator it outputs a shape tree, so it goes through sRender, and it can be passed through modifiers such as sRound, sOffset or sWriteOn first. Its Transform tab positions, rotates and scales the shape, and its Style tab sets the fill and outline. Both are described under Common Controls → Krokodove tools.

**Use for:** quick graphic elements such as crosses, stars, plus and bullet markers, and polygon badges, which then get modifiers and styling in the shape chain.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Type | `Type` | Combo | 0 (0: Cross, 1: Polygon, 2: Rectangle, 3: Star) | The primitive to create. |
| Size X, Size Y | `SizeX`, `SizeY` | Number | 0.5, 0.25 (0–1) | Width and height of the primitive, in shape units. For a cross, Size X sets the arm length and Size Y the arm thickness. |
| Steps | `Steps` | Number | 4 (3–16) | Sides for Polygon and points for Star. Cross and Rectangle ignore it. |
| Angle | `Angle` | Number | 0.5 (0–360, degrees) | Rotation of the primitive about its centre. |

### Example

A five-pointed star, given rounded corners and rendered over the video:

```python
star = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapePrimitiveCreate')
star.Type = 3                           # Star
star.Steps = 5
star.SizeX = 0.4
star.SizeY = 0.4

rnd = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapeRound')
rnd.Input = star.Output
rnd.Radius = 0.02

render = comp.AddTool('sRender')
render.Input = rnd.Output

merge = comp.AddTool('Merge')
merge.Background = media_in.Output
merge.Foreground = render.Output
```

### Tips

- Set Type to Polygon and Steps to 6 for a hexagon, or to 32 for a near-circle. Polygon is an ellipse drawn with Steps segments: equal sizes give a regular polygon, and unequal sizes stretch it.
- For a cross, make Size Y smaller than Size X for thin arms, and equal sizes for blunt arms.
- Animate Angle to spin the primitive. The Transform tab's Rotation does the same for any shape.

**See also:** sSpiral Create, sTrace Create, sRound, sOffset, sWriteOn, sRender, sRectangle, sStar, sNGon.

## sSpiral Create (`KD_ShapeSpiralCreate`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape Create · **Short name:** sSpiC · **Inputs:** none · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Generates an open spiral, as a line that winds from a start radius to an end radius over a range of angles. The radius changes evenly from RadiusStart to RadiusEnd while the angle runs from Angle Start to Angle End, and Angle Step sets how finely the path is divided. Angle End Type decides how the last turn is closed off. The spiral is a plain path, so it can be written on, offset into rings or styled like any other shape.

**Use for:** spiral wipes and swirl graphics, a spiral line that draws on, and the spiral form of a loop or shell.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Radius Start | `RadiusStart` | Number | 0.1 (0–1) | Radius at the start of the spiral, in shape units. |
| Radius End | `RadiusEnd` | Number | 0.3 (0–2) | Radius at the end of the spiral. |
| Angle Start | `AngleStart` | Number | 0 (degrees) | Angle where the spiral starts. |
| Angle End | `AngleEnd` | Number | 720 (degrees) | Angle where the spiral ends. The default is two full turns. |
| Angle Step | `AngleStep` | Number | 20 (0.5–90, degrees) | Angle between points of the spiral. Smaller steps give a smoother curve and more points. |
| Angle End Type | `AngleEndType` | Multi-button | 1 (0: None, 1: Type 1, 2: Type 2) | How the last partial step is closed. None stops at the last full step. Type 1 ends at RadiusEnd. Type 2 ends at the radius the spiral would have reached at that angle. |

### Example

A two-turn spiral that draws on, rendered and merged over the video:

```python
spiral = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapeSpiralCreate')
spiral.RadiusStart = 0.02
spiral.RadiusEnd = 0.35
spiral.AngleEnd = 720
spiral.AngleStep = 10

write = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapeWriteOn')
write.Input = spiral.Output
write.RangeEnd = comp.BezierSpline()
write.RangeEnd[0] = 0.0
write.RangeEnd[48] = 1.0

render = comp.AddTool('sRender')
render.Input = write.Output

merge = comp.AddTool('Merge')
merge.Background = media_in.Output
merge.Foreground = render.Output
```

### Tips

- Set RadiusStart to 0 for a spiral that winds out from a centre point.
- A smaller Angle Step gives a smoother spiral with more points. A large step shows visible corners.
- The direction follows the angles: when Angle End is less than Angle Start, the spiral winds the other way.
- Animate Angle End to grow the spiral turn by turn.

**See also:** sPrimitive Create, sTrace Create, sWriteOn, sSmooth, sOffset, sRender, sEllipse.

## sTrace Create (`KD_ShapeTraceCreate`)

**Category:** Krokodove: Shape Create · **Short name:** sTraC · **Inputs:** `Image` (Image) · **Output:** `Output` (ShapeTree)

Traces the outline of a picture into a vector shape. The image's chosen channel is compared with Threshold, and every area above the threshold becomes a filled region whose outline is the shape. Use it to turn a logo, a mask or a rendered silhouette into shapes that can then be written on, offset, zigzagged or styled. The trace is made from the image's own pixels, so a sharp, high-contrast source gives the cleanest result. The Transform tab moves and scales the traced shape, as on the other create tools.

**Use for:** turning a logo, a hand-drawn scan or a matte into editable outlines, and building write-on graphics from existing artwork.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Image | `Image` | Image input | none | The picture to trace. Connect any image output, such as a Media In or a rendered mask. |
| Map Channel | `MapChannel` | Multi-button | 4 (0: Red, 1: Green, 2: Blue, 3: Alpha, 4: Luminance) | The channel of the image that is compared with Threshold. Use Alpha for a shape already cut out, or Luminance for a black-and-white graphic. |
| Threshold | `Threshold` | Number | 0.5 (0–1) | Pixels whose channel value is above this are inside the traced shape. Lower values include more of the image. |
| Curve Precision | `CurvePrecision` | Number | 8 (2–16) | How finely the traced outline is simplified into curves. Higher values follow fine detail more closely. |

### Example

Trace the luminance of a picture into an outline, write it on, then render and merge it over the video:

```python
trace = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapeTraceCreate')
trace.Image = media_in.Output
trace.MapChannel = 4                    # Luminance
trace.Threshold = 0.4

write = comp.AddTool('KD_ShapeWriteOn')
write.Input = trace.Output
write.RangeEnd = comp.BezierSpline()
write.RangeEnd[0] = 0.0
write.RangeEnd[60] = 1.0

render = comp.AddTool('sRender')
render.Input = write.Output

merge = comp.AddTool('Merge')
merge.Background = media_in.Output
merge.Foreground = render.Output
```

### Tips

- Start with Threshold around 0.5. If the traced shape is too heavy, raise Threshold. If it is missing detail, lower it.
- For a matte or a clean logo, use Alpha as the map channel. Luminance works for black-on-white graphics.
- A traced outline is a filled shape. For an outline effect, run it through sOutline first.
- The trace is positioned at the centre of the frame. Use the Transform tab to move it.

**See also:** sPrimitive Create, sSpiral Create, sOutline, sWriteOn, sRender, sZigZag, Merge.

## B-Spline (`NURBSpline`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** none · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to a Number input) · **Output:** `Value` (Number)

A smoothed animation curve for a number. Unlike BezierSpline, the curve does not pass through its keys: each key pulls
the curve towards it, so the curve is softer and the value at a key can differ from the key value. Keys have weights
that set how strongly each one pulls, edited in the Spline Editor (hold W and drag a point). Its name is "B-Spline" in
the UI. Not to be confused with BSpline, the B-spline shape data type, which can't be attached to a Number input.

**Use for:** smooth, organic movement where exact hits on the keys don't matter, such as drifting or floating motion.

Attach it by assigning it to an input, then set keys with `input[frame] = value`, as for BezierSpline. Its keys are
read back with `GetKeyFrames()`, which returns only the frame numbers (no values or handles).

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (none) | | | | The spline has no Inspector controls. Edit it in the Spline Editor. |

### Example

```python
xf = comp.AddTool('Transform')
xf.Size = comp.NURBSpline()
xf.Size[0] = 0.0
xf.Size[12] = 1.0
xf.Size[24] = 0.0
print(xf.Size[12])   # not 1.0: the curve is pulled towards the key, not pinned to it
```

### Tips

- Use BezierSpline when a key must be hit exactly. Use Cubic Spline when the curve should pass through the keys but
  with a different easing.
- Key values are read back by reading the input at each frame, since GetKeyFrames gives no values here.

**See also:** BezierSpline, Cubic Spline, Natural Cubic Spline, BSpline Path, Modifiers overview.

## Beat (`KD_NumberBeat`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** Beat · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to a Number input) · **Output:** `Number` (Number)

Produces a repeating envelope: from Minimum Value it rises to Maximum Value over the Attack time, falls to Sustain Value over the Decay time, holds for the Sustain time, then falls back to Minimum Value over the Release time. The envelope repeats once per beat. A beat is set either as a number of frames or as a tempo in beats per minute with a frame rate. Start and End time limit the envelope to a part of the timeline, and the result can be combined with a value by addition, multiplication, or a maximum or minimum.

**Use for:** pulsing a size, opacity or position in time with music, and any regular rhythm, such as a title that beats on each bar.

Modifiers are not added with AddTool. Connect one to an input, as in the example, and reach its controls through the input, as shown there.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Rate Type | `RateType` | Multi-button | 0 (0: Frames/Beat, 1: Beats/Minute (BPM)) | How the beat length is given. |
| Frequency | `Frequency` | Number | 10 (0–100) | Frames per beat. Used when Rate Type is Frames/Beat. |
| Beats per Minute | `BeatsperMinute` | Number | 120 (0.0001–240) | Tempo. Used when Rate Type is BPM. |
| Frames per Second | `FramesperSecond` | Number | 25 (0.0001–30) | Frame rate used to turn BPM into frames. Used when Rate Type is BPM. |
| Start time | `Starttime` | Number | 0 (0–100) | Frame at which the envelope starts. |
| End time | `Endtime` | Number | 1000 (0–1000) | Frame after which the envelope stops. |
| Round to Full Beat Cycle | `RoundtoFullBeatCycle` | Checkbox | 1 | Extends End time to the end of the beat it falls in. |
| Attack time | `Attacktime` | Number | 2 (0–10) | Frames to rise from Minimum to Maximum. |
| Decay Time | `DecayTime` | Number | 2 (0–10) | Frames to fall from Maximum to Sustain. |
| Sustain Time | `SustainTime` | Number | 2 (0–10) | Frames to hold at Sustain. |
| Release Time | `ReleaseTime` | Number | 2 (0–10) | Frames to fall from Sustain to Minimum. |
| Interpolation | `Interpolation` | Multi-button | 1 (0: Linear, 1: Ease-in, Ease-out) | Listed in the Inspector, but has no effect in the current source. The envelope is always linear, as the example's values show. |
| Maximum Value | `MaximumValue` | Number | 1 (0–1) | The peak of the envelope. |
| Sustain Value | `SustainValue` | Number | 0.5 (0–1) | The level held during Sustain. |
| Minimum Value | `MinimumValue` | Number | 0 (0–1) | The level between beats. |
| Combine Value | `CombineValue` | Multi-button | 0 (0: Add, 1: Multiply, 2: Maximum, 3: Minimum) | How the Value below is combined with the envelope. |
| Value | `Value` | Number | 0 (0–1) | The number combined with the envelope. |

### Example

A title that pulses on each beat of a 120 BPM track at 25 frames per second: it jumps to 1.15 and falls back to 1 within each beat (12.5 frames).

```python
title = comp.AddTool('Transform')
title.Size = comp.KD_NumberBeat()           # a modifier, connected to Size

beat = title.Size.GetConnectedOutput().GetTool()   # reach the modifier
beat.RateType = 1                           # Beats/Minute
beat.BeatsperMinute = 120
beat.FramesperSecond = 25                   # 12.5 frames per beat
beat.MaximumValue = 0.15                    # the pulse peaks at 0.15
beat.SustainValue = 0.0                     # and falls back to zero
beat.Attacktime = 1
beat.DecayTime = 3
beat.SustainTime = 0
beat.ReleaseTime = 5
beat.Value = 1.0
beat.CombineValue = 0                       # Add: size = 1 + envelope
```

### Tips

- Outside Start time and End time the envelope is zero, so the output is just Value combined with zero.
- With Rate Type Frames/Beat, the beat length is Frequency. The four phase times must fit inside the beat, or the later phases are cut off.
- Use Combine Value Multiply with Value 1 to scale an input by the envelope, rather than add to it.
- Interpolation has no effect, so shape the envelope with the phase times and levels instead.

**See also:** Random (`KD_NumberRandom`), Color Switcher (`KD_NumberColorSwitchboard`), Modifiers overview, Transform.

## BezierSpline (`BezierSpline`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** none · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to a Number input) · **Output:** `Value` (Number)

The default animation curve for a number. Each key has a value and two Bézier handles, which set how the curve
leaves and enters that key, so each key can be smooth, eased or sharp. Keys are edited in the Spline Editor, which
shows the curve; from a script you set keys on the input, as in the example. The curve has no Inspector controls.

**Use for:** keyframed animation of any Number input, from simple fades to eased motion. Also the spline that a
Path or XY Path uses for its displacement or X and Y curves.

Attach it by assigning it to an input, before setting keys: without a modifier, `input[frame] = value` just changes the
constant value. The other spline types (B-Spline, Cubic Spline, Natural Cubic Spline) are the same kind of modifier and
differ only in how the curve passes through the keys. See Cubic Spline.

### Example

A value that rises from 0.5 at frame 0 to 1.5 at frame 24, then falls to 1.0 at frame 48. The keys are new, so
they are linear (see below):

```python
xf = comp.AddTool('Transform')
xf.Size = comp.BezierSpline()          # a Bézier spline connected to Size
xf.Size[0] = 0.5
xf.Size[24] = 1.5
xf.Size[48] = 1.0

spl = xf.Size.GetConnectedOutput().GetTool()   # the spline modifier
print(spl.GetKeyFrames())                       # {0.0: {1: 0.5, 'RH': {...}}, 24.0: {...}, 48.0: {...}}
```

### Key frames from script

These are the verified ways to read and write a spline's keys from external Python. The spline is the modifier
returned by `input.GetConnectedOutput().GetTool()`.

**Read.** `spl.GetKeyFrames()` returns a dict keyed by frame (a float):
`{frame: {1: value, 'LH': {1: dx, 2: dy}, 'RH': {1: dx, 2: dy}}}`. `1` is the key value. `LH` and `RH` are the
left and right handles as offsets from the key: `dx` is in frames (negative for LH) and `dy` is in value units. The
first key has only `RH` and the last only `LH`. Every key has handles in the readback, whether you set them or not.
For a linear key the handles lie on the line to the neighbouring keys.

```python
for frame, key in sorted(spl.GetKeyFrames().items()):
    print(frame, key[1], key.get('LH'), key.get('RH'))
```

The value at any frame, interpolated, is `xf.Size[frame]`.

**Write the whole curve.** `spl.SetKeyFrames({frame: key, ...})` replaces every key on the spline: keys not in the dict
are removed. Give handles to shape the curve, or leave them out to get automatic handles:

```python
spl.SetKeyFrames({
    0.0:  {1: 0.0, 'RH': {1: 8.0, 2: 0.0}},                              # flat (eased) start
    24.0: {1: 1.0, 'LH': {1: -8.0, 2: 0.0}, 'RH': {1: 8.0, 2: 0.0}},    # flat at the peak
    48.0: {1: 0.0, 'LH': {1: -8.0, 2: 0.0}},                            # flat (eased) end
})
```

With flat handles on a 0-to-1 move over 24 frames, frame 6 reads 0.156 (eased) rather than 0.25 (linear). A second
argument (`SetKeyFrames(keys, True)`) makes no difference.

**Change one key.** Assigning to the input adds or replaces one key and keeps the others: `xf.Size[36] = 0.6` (or
`xf.SetInput('Size', 0.6, 36)`). The new key gets automatic handles, and the neighbouring keys' automatic handles are
recalculated.

**Delete a key.** `spl.DeleteKeyFrames(24.0)` removes the key at that frame. A frame with no key is ignored. Setting a
key's value to `None` does not delete it; use `DeleteKeyFrames`.

**Key type (linear by default).** New keys are linear unless the `Comp.Splines.AutoSmoothSplines` preference is on, in
which case they are smooth. A key set from script keeps the handles you give it, as shown above. From a script you
can't yet set a key's type to Linear, Smooth or Step (hold). A `'Flags'` entry in a key dict is accepted but ignored and
not read back, and `spl.AdjustKeyFrames` did not change a key when tested. Setting key flags, loop and AdjustKeyFrames
are API gaps for now. Daniel plans an `INPS_SplineType` input attribute (Default, Linear, Smooth, StepIn, StepOut) to
get and set the key type per input; this section will change when it lands. Ease In/Out presets are only in the
Spline Editor. Use explicit handles, as in the example, for eased or straight segments.

### Tips

- Keys are added at the frame you set them. Use whole frames for clean keys; fractional frames such as 24.5 also work.
- To retime a whole animation at once, use Keyframe Stretcher.
- Use `SetKeyFrames` when you rebuild a curve in one go, and `input[frame] = value` for single edits.

**See also:** B-Spline, Cubic Spline, Natural Cubic Spline, Path, XY Path, Keyframe Stretcher, Modifiers overview.

## BSpline (`BSpline`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** none · **Inputs:** none · **Output:** none in the toolset dump

The B-spline shape type, the curve used by B-spline shapes such as the B-Spline mask. It is not a number modifier:
`tool.AddModifier('Size', 'BSpline')` returns False, so it can't be attached to a Number input. Its curve is drawn and
edited in the viewer and Spline Editor, as with other shapes. Its name is close to B-Spline (`NURBSpline`), which is the
number animation modifier. Use that one to animate a value.

**Use for:** shape data (the B-Spline mask's curve). For animating a number, use B-Spline (`NURBSpline`) or BezierSpline.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (none) | | | | The type has no Inspector controls. |

### Tips

- Don't search for this type in the Modifiers menu when you want animation: use B-Spline (`NURBSpline`).

**See also:** B-Spline (`NURBSpline`), BSpline Path, Path.

## BSpline Path (`BSplinePath`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** none · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to a Point input) · **Output:** `Position` (Point), `Heading` (Number)

A motion path like Path, for a Point input, whose curve is B-spline smoothed rather than passing through its points.
The controls are the same as Path's, with the addition of Show View Controls, which hides the on-screen controls.

**Use for:** a smooth, drifting path where the points are guides rather than exact stops.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Show View Controls | `ShowViewControls` | Checkbox | 1 | Shows the path's on-screen controls in the viewer. |
| Center | `Center` | Point | (0.5, 0.5) | Moves the whole path. |
| Size | `Size` | Number | 1 (slider 0–5) | Scales the path. |
| X Rotation | `XRotation` | Number | 0 (0–360) | Rotates the path around the X axis. |
| Y Rotation | `YRotation` | Number | 0 (0–360) | Rotates the path around the Y axis. |
| Z Rotation | `ZRotation` | Number | 0 (0–360) | Rotates the path around the Z axis. |
| Displacement | `Displacement` | Number | 0 (0–1) | The position along the path: 0 at the start and 1 at the end. Connected to a spline by default. |
| Heading Offset | `HeadingOffset` | Number | 0 (0–360) | Adds to the Heading output. |

The points are keyed on the input, as with Path, with `input[frame] = [x, y]`. The example in Path applies, with
BSplinePath in place of PolyPath (not run separately).

**See also:** Path, B-Spline (`NURBSpline`), XY Path, BezierSpline.

## Calculation (`Calculation`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** Calc · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to a Number input) · **Output:** `Result` (Number)

Combines two numbers with one operation and outputs the result. The two operands can be set as constants or driven by their own time scale and offset, so each side can follow a different timing. Use it for quick maths between a value and a constant, or between two inputs.

**Use for:** scaling or offsetting an animated value, averaging two values, taking the larger or smaller of two, and combining two values into an input without writing a formula.

Calculation is a modifier: it isn't added with AddTool. Attach it with `AddModifier` and reach its controls through the input, as shown in the example.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| First Operand | `FirstOperand` | Number | 0 (0–1) | The first number in the operation. |
| Operator | `Operator` | Combo | 0 (0: Add, 1: Subtract (First - Second), 2: Multiply, 3: Divide (First / Second), 4: Divide (Second / First), 5: Subtract (Second - First), 6: Minimum, 7: Maximum, 8: Average, 9: First Only, 10: Second Only, 11: Add Random, 12: Multiply Random, 13: Modulo (First % Second), 14: Modulo (Second % First), 15: Difference, 16: Power (First ^ Second), 17: Power (Second ^ First)) | The operation to apply. |
| Second Operand | `SecondOperand` | Number | 0 (0–1) | The second number in the operation. |
| First Operand Time Scale | `FirstOperandTimeScale` | Number | 1 (0–5) | Speeds up or slows down the first operand's time. |
| First Operand Time Offset | `FirstOperandTimeOffset` | Number | 0 (0–100) | Shifts the first operand in time. |
| Second Operand Time Scale | `SecondOperandTimeScale` | Number | 1 (0–5) | Speeds up or slows down the second operand's time. |
| Second Operand Time Offset | `SecondOperandTimeOffset` | Number | 0 (0–100) | Shifts the second operand in time. |

### Example

A value of 0.3 averaged with 0.2 (the Average option), driving a Transform's Size.

```python
xf = comp.AddTool('Transform')
xf.AddModifier('Size', 'Calculation')
calc = xf.Size.GetConnectedOutput().GetTool()   # the modifier

calc.FirstOperand = 0.3
calc.SecondOperand = 0.2
calc.Operator = 8                               # Average: 0.25
```

### Tips

- Set Operator with its index (0-based). The option names are in the table.
- Reading the value per frame is the quickest check: `xf.Size[0]` gives 0.25 in the example.
- To use the result on an input without a modifier, assign its output: `xf.Size = calc.Result` (keep the tool in a variable, as `calc = comp.Calculation()`). Verified: the input connects and follows the operands.
- To animate an operand, connect a spline to it, as on any Number input. Not verified on this modifier.
- For a formula instead of a fixed operation, use Expression (`Expression`).

**See also:** Expression (`Expression`), Publish (`Publish*`), Random (`KD_NumberRandom`), Transform (`Transform`).

## Character Level Styling (`StyledTextCLS`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** Char Style · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to the StyledText input of a Text+) · **Output:** `StyledText` (Text)

Changes the style of selected characters in a Text+ only: their colour, size, offset, rotation and shading. It works on a selection made in the Inspector, and the rest of the text keeps the Text+ settings. The controls match the Text+ Transform and Shading tabs, with the character selection made in the viewer or Inspector.

**Use for:** highlighting one word or letter in a title, and changing a few characters' size or colour in a line.

Character Level Styling is a modifier: it isn't added with AddTool. Attach it to a Text+ with `AddModifier`.

| Control | ID | Type | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| Right-click Here to Animate Character Level Styling | `CharacterLevelStyling` | Label | The control to start a character-level styling animation, in the Inspector. Not scriptable here. |
| Clear Selected Character Styling | `ClearSelectedStyling` | Button | Removes the styling from the selected characters. Not verified. |
| Clear All Character Styling | `ClearAllStyling` | Button | Removes all character-level styling. Not verified. |
| Transform, Shading and Text controls | as on Text+ and Follower | | The values applied to the selected characters. See Text+ (`TextPlus`) and Follower (`StyledTextFollower`) for the IDs. |

### Example

Attaching Character Level Styling to a Text+. The text passes through unchanged until characters are styled.

```python
title = comp.AddTool('TextPlus')
title.StyledText = 'ABCDEFGH'
title.AddModifier('StyledText', 'StyledTextCLS')
```

Verified: the modifier attaches, and the Text+ reads 'ABCDEFGH'. Selecting characters and setting their styling is not verified from script: the selection is made in the viewer, and this reference has no way to do it.

### Tips

- Apply the styling in the viewer for a fixed selection, and script the rest of the title.
- Use Follower (`StyledTextFollower`) to animate every character, and CLS for a few.

**See also:** Follower (`StyledTextFollower`), Text+ (`TextPlus`), TextScramble (`TextScramble`).

## Color Switcher (`KD_NumberColorSwitchboard`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** CSw · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect one of its outputs to a Number or colour channel) · **Outputs:** `Number` (Number), and `R1`…`R8`, `G1`…`G8`, `B1`…`B8` (Number each)

Holds up to eight palettes, called Sets, of up to eight colours each. At each frame it chooses one Set and outputs its colours in eight slots, as red, green and blue numbers. Remap sets which colour fills each slot, and Cycle Range with Cycle Offset rotates the slots through the palette. `Number` is the red value of slot 1.

**Use for:** switching a whole colour scheme with one control, animating a palette change, and cycling colours through a set of slots, such as a set of bars or letters that each take a different colour.

Modifiers are not added with AddTool. Connect one of its outputs to an input, as in the example, and reach its controls through that input.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Set | `Set` | Number | 1 (1–8) | The palette in use. |
| Cycle Range | `CycleRange` | Number | 8 (2–8) | How many slots take part in the cycle. |
| Cycle Offset | `CycleOffset` | Number | 0 (0–8) | Rotates the slots within the cycle range. Animate it to move colours along the slots. |
| Remap 1–8 | `Remap1` … `Remap8` | Number | 1 to 8 (1–8) | Which colour of the Set fills each slot. Remap 1 is slot 1, and so on. |
| Colours | `Color11Red` … `Color88Alpha` | Color | varies | Red, Green, Blue and Alpha of each colour. The digits are the Set, then the colour, so `Color11` is Set 1, colour 1, and `Color88` is Set 8, colour 8. |

### Example

A two-colour palette that changes from blue to red over frames 0 to 24.

```python
palette = comp.KD_NumberColorSwitchboard()

bg = comp.AddTool('Background')
bg.TopLeftRed = palette.R1
bg.TopLeftGreen = palette.G1
bg.TopLeftBlue = palette.B1

sw = bg.TopLeftRed.GetConnectedOutput().GetTool()   # reach the modifier
sw.Color11Red = 0.0                                 # Set 1, colour 1: blue
sw.Color11Green = 0.2
sw.Color11Blue = 1.0
sw.Color21Red = 1.0                                 # Set 2, colour 1: red
sw.Color21Green = 0.1
sw.Color21Blue = 0.1
sw.Set = comp.BezierSpline()                        # animate the Set control
sw.Set[0] = 1
sw.Set[24] = 2                                      # Set 2 from about frame 12
```

### Tips

- Set and the Remap controls are whole numbers from 1 to 8. A keyframed Set jumps to the nearest whole number between keys, so it switches halfway between two keys.
- Use Cycle Offset with a keyframed value to march a colour pattern across a row of slots.
- Each colour's alpha channel exists, but the outputs are only red, green and blue.
- The modifier has no image output. It drives numeric or colour-channel inputs, so connect each channel you need.

**See also:** Random (`KD_NumberRandom`), Beat (`KD_NumberBeat`), Modifiers overview, Background.

## CompName (`CompName`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** Comp Name · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to the StyledText input of a Text+) · **Output:** `Name` (Text)

Outputs the name of the composition as text. It has no controls. Use it to show the comp's name in a title or slate without typing it.

**Use for:** slates and labels that should match the comp's name.

CompName is a modifier: it isn't added with AddTool. Attach it to a Text+ with `AddModifier`, and the Text+ shows the comp name.

It has no controls to set. Read the Text+'s text to get the name.

### Example

A title that shows the comp's name.

```python
title = comp.AddTool('TextPlus')
title.AddModifier('StyledText', 'CompName')
name_text = title.StyledText[0]                         # the comp's name
```

Verified: the Text+ reads the comp name as its text (in a scratch comp this was 'Composition38', the scratch comp's own name).

### Tips

- The name comes from the composition, so renaming the comp changes the text.

**See also:** TimeCode (`TimeCode`), TextTimer (`TextTimer`), Text+ (`TextPlus`).

## CoordTransform 3D (`CoordTransform3D`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** 3CX · **Inputs:** `TargetObject` (a 3D object, DataType3D), `SceneInput` (a 3D scene) · **Output:** `Output` (DataType3D), `Position.X`, `Position.Y`, `Position.Z` (Number)

Gives the position of a 3D object, as numbers, so other controls can follow it. It attaches to the XYZ controls of a 3D
transform, and the object is connected as TargetObject. The modifier's own Transform3DOp controls move or rotate the
coordinates it reads, and its outputs carry the transformed position.

**Use for:** driving a 2D or 3D control from where a 3D object sits in the scene, such as a label that follows a model
through a Camera 3D.

### Example

Attached to the X offset of a Transform 3D, with a Cube 3D as the target:

```python
cube = comp.AddTool('Cube3D')
xf = comp.AddTool('Transform3D')
xf.AddModifier('Transform3DOp.Translate.X', 'CoordTransform3D')

ct = xf['Transform3DOp.Translate.X'].GetConnectedOutput().GetTool()   # the modifier
ct.TargetObject = cube.Output       # the 3D object to read
ct.SubID = 0
```

### Tips

- It is also a tool: `comp.CoordTransform3D()` and `comp.AddTool('CoordTransform3D', ...)` both create it, with
  outputs `Output` (3D data) and `Position.X`, `Position.Y`, `Position.Z`.
- Attached to a Transform 3D's X offset, its main output is 3D data, so the connection is for the scene, not for a number.
  Reading `Position.X` as a value from a script was not verified (scratch comps can't render 3D positions in this session).
- Use `Transform3DOp.*` IDs as in the table; the dotted name is what `AddModifier` accepts. `Transform3DOp.Translate.X` is
  the verified one.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Target Object | `TargetObject` | DataType3D | none | The 3D object whose position is read. |
| Scene Input | `SceneInput` | DataType3D | none | The scene the object belongs to. |
| Sub ID | `SubID` | Number | 0 (0–10, integer) | Chooses one object in the target when it contains several. |
| X Offset | `Transform3DOp.Translate.X` | Number | 0 (-2 to 2) | Adds to the X position. |
| Y Offset | `Transform3DOp.Translate.Y` | Number | 0 (-2 to 2) | Adds to the Y position. |
| Z Offset | `Transform3DOp.Translate.Z` | Number | 0 (-10 to 10) | Adds to the Z position. |

The Rotation, Pivot, Scale and Target controls are the same as on the Transform 3D tool; see that section.

**See also:** Transform 3D, Camera 3D, Vector, Offset, Modifiers overview.

## Cubic Spline (`CubicSpline`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** none · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to a Number input) · **Output:** `Value` (Number)

An animation curve for a number that passes through its keys, with smooth curves between them. Like the other spline
modifiers, it has no Inspector controls: it is edited in the Spline Editor. The manual's menu path is a little misleading
(it names Natural Cubic Spline under Cubic Spline); the two are separate modifiers here.

**Use for:** smooth animation that hits every key, with easing decided by the neighbouring keys.

Attach it by assigning it to an input, then set keys with `input[frame] = value`. Keys are read back with
`GetKeyFrames()` as frame numbers only.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| (none) | | | | The spline has no Inspector controls. |

### Example

```python
xf = comp.AddTool('Transform')
xf.Size = comp.CubicSpline()
xf.Size[0] = 0.0
xf.Size[12] = 1.0
xf.Size[24] = 0.0
print(xf.Size[12])   # 1.0: the curve passes through the key
```

**See also:** Natural Cubic Spline, B-Spline (`NURBSpline`), BezierSpline.

## Custom Poly (`CustomPoly`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** Custom Poly · **Inputs:** Source Polyline, Source Polyline 2 and 3 (Polyline), Source Image (Image) · **Output:** `Output` (Polyline)

Builds a polyline whose points are set by formulas in X and Y, over a number of points. Its inputs are the Point and Number inputs (`p1`…`p9`, `n1`…`n9`), and it can also start from a source polyline. The formulas and how they read these inputs are not verified in detail here.

**Use for:** shapes that follow a formula, and polylines that depend on other inputs.

Custom Poly is a modifier that outputs a polyline. The controls are described here, and no example is given.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number of Points | `NumPoints` | Number | 20 (0–100) | The number of points on the line. |
| Poly Expression X | `PolyExpressionX` | Text | "px" | The formula for the X position of each point. |
| Poly Expression Y | `PolyExpressionY` | Text | "py" | The formula for the Y position of each point. |
| Source Polyline | `SourcePolyline` | Polyline | | A polyline to build from. Connect a polyline shape here, or set one (see *Value types* in Conventions). |
| Source Image | `SourceImage` | Image | | An image the formulas can read. |
| Number In 1–9 | `n1`…`n9` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Numbers the formulas can read. |
| Point In 1–9 | `p1`…`p9` | Point | (0.5, 0.5) | Points the formulas can read. |

### Tips

- Connect the output to a polyline input of a shape, such as a mask, to see the result in the viewer.
- No example is given, since the formulas are not verified here.

**See also:** Expression (`Expression`), Polygon Mask (`Polygon`), Calculation (`Calculation`).

## Expression (`Expression`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** Expr · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect its outputs to a Number or Point input) · **Output:** `NumberResult` (Number) and `PointResult` (Point)

Evaluates a formula for each frame, from up to nine Number inputs (`n1`…`n9`) and nine Point inputs (`p1`…`p9`). The Number formula gives `NumberResult`; the X and Y formulas give `PointResult`. The formulas are Lua expressions, with `time` for the current frame. Use it when a value depends on other values or on time, and a plain keyframe curve isn't enough.

**Use for:** linking one value to another (with a scale or offset), oscillating motion from `time`, and combining several inputs into one number or point.

Expression is a modifier: it isn't added with AddTool. Create it with `comp.Expression()`, which makes a tool named `Expression1`, and connect its outputs to the input you want to drive. Per-input expressions, without a modifier, are described under *Expressions* below.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Number Expression | `NumberExpression` | Text | "" | The formula for `NumberResult`. Use `n1`…`n9` and `time`. |
| Point Expression X | `PointExpressionX` | Text | "" | The formula for the X value of `PointResult`. Names the Point and Number inputs as `p1x`, `p2x`… and `n1`, and uses `time`. |
| Point Expression Y | `PointExpressionY` | Text | "" | The formula for the Y value of `PointResult`, named as `p1y`, `p2y`… A blank formula gives 0.0. |
| Number In 1–9 | `n1`…`n9` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Number inputs, named in the formula as `n1`…`n9`. Used in NumberExpression. |
| Point In 1–9 | `p1`…`p9` | Point | (0.5, 0.5) | Point inputs, named in the formula as `p1`…`p9`. Used in the Point expressions. |
| Random Seed | `RandomSeed` | Number | 0 (0–1000) | The seed setting for the modifier. Its effect on formulas is not verified. |
| Reseed | `Randomize` | Button | | Picks a new random seed. Not verified. |

### Example

A value that rises with time and is scaled by a number input, driving a Transform's Size.

```python
expr = comp.Expression()                  # the modifier: makes Expression1
expr.NumberExpression = 'n1*2 + time/100'
expr.n1 = 0.25

xf = comp.AddTool('Transform')
xf.Size = expr.NumberResult               # 0.5 at frame 0, 1.0 at frame 50
```

Setting `xf.Size = expr.NumberResult` connects the output. Assigning `expr` itself, as in `xf.Size = expr`, doesn't connect it, and `AddModifier` doesn't accept Expression (it returns False). Connect `PointResult` the same way: `xf.Center = expr.PointResult` (verified). `PointExpressionX` and `PointExpressionY` set the two parts of the point, as in the Point example below.

### Point output

A point built from two formulas, driving a Transform's Center. Verified: with `p1` at [0.2, 0.4] and X = `p1x + 0.1`, the point reads {1: 0.3, 2: 0.4} at every frame. The X formula `p1x * 2 + time/100` gives 0.4 at frame 0 and 0.9 at frame 50.

```python
expr = comp.Expression()
expr.p1 = [0.2, 0.4]
expr.PointExpressionX = 'p1x + 0.1'             # X: 0.3
expr.PointExpressionY = 'p1y'                   # Y: 0.4

xf = comp.AddTool('Transform')
xf.Center = expr.PointResult
```

Read the formula back with `expr.GetInput('PointExpressionX')`. The plain `expr.PointExpressionX` attribute returns an object, not the text.

### Expressions

An input can take a formula directly, without a modifier, with `SetExpression`. The formula is evaluated for each frame, and the input's own value is ignored while it's set. These are verified in a scratch comp:

```python
xf = comp.AddTool('Transform')
xf.Size.SetExpression('0.5 + 0.25*math.sin(time/10)')   # time is the frame number
print(xf.Size.GetExpression())                           # reads the formula back
xf.Size.SetExpression(None)                              # clears it; Size reverts to its default (1.0)
```

- **Other tools.** Refer to a tool by its name, with its input after a dot: `src = comp.AddTool('Transform')`, then `xf2.Size.SetExpression(src.Name + '.Size * 2')`. The `comp.` prefix (`comp.Transform1.Size`) doesn't work in a formula. The result follows the other tool when its value changes.
- **Points.** A Point input takes a formula that returns two numbers: `xf.Center.SetExpression('{0.5 + 0.2*math.sin(time/10), 0.5}')`, or `Point(x, y)`, which is valid inside a formula. `GetExpression` returns the text, and the value reads as `{1: x, 2: y, 3: 0.0}`. A formula can also name another tool's Point, such as `Transform1.Center`.
- **Clearing.** `SetExpression(None)` removes the formula and restores the input's default. `SetExpression('')` does not clear: it leaves an empty formula that evaluates to 0.0. Setting a constant (`xf.Size = 0.9`) or calling `SetInput` does not remove a formula either, so use `SetExpression(None)` first.
- **Keyframes.** A BezierSpline or PolyPath connected to the input is kept when a formula is set, and comes back when the formula is cleared with `SetExpression(None)`. While a formula is set, it overrides the spline.
- **Errors.** A formula with a syntax error is accepted and returned by `GetExpression`, but the value reads as None. Check the value after setting a formula.

### Tips

- Use `time` for the current frame, and divide to slow things down (`time/100`).
- A modifier (`comp.Expression()`) is better when several inputs need one formula, or the formula needs visible controls. A per-input formula is quicker for one-off links.
- Read the value with `xf.Size[frame]` to check a formula without rendering.
- Don't use `SetExpression('')` to clear. It leaves a formula that returns 0.0.

**See also:** Calculation (`Calculation`), Publish (`Publish*`), Switch (modifier) (`Switch*`), Random (`KD_NumberRandom`), Transform (`Transform`).

## Fairlight Animator (`FairlightAnimator`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** Fairlight · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to a Number input) · **Output:** `Value` (Number)

Drives a Number input from an audio analysis made in the Fairlight page of DaVinci Resolve, such as the loudness of a clip. You pick the clip and the analysis, then scale and offset the result. The analysis is made in Resolve, so the modifier shows nothing useful in a scratch comp.

**Use for:** pulsing titles and graphics with the sound of a clip.

Fairlight Animator is a modifier: it isn't added with AddTool. Attach it with `AddModifier`. The clip and analysis need to exist in Resolve.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Clip Name | `ClipName` | Text | "" | The name of the audio clip to analyse. |
| Media ID | `MediaID` | Text | "" | The media ID of the clip. |
| Analysis | `Analysis` | ID combo | (none) | The analysis to read. The options are chosen in the Inspector; the list isn't in the dump. |
| Scale | `Scale` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Multiplies the result. |
| Offset | `Offset` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Added to the result. |
| Time Scale | `TimeScale` | Number | 1 (0–1) | Speeds up or slows down the analysis time. |
| Time Offset | `TimeOffset` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Shifts the analysis time. |

### Example

Attaching the modifier and setting its scale.

```python
xf = comp.AddTool('Transform')
xf.AddModifier('Size', 'FairlightAnimator')
fa = xf.Size.GetConnectedOutput().GetTool()   # the modifier

fa.Scale = 0.5
fa.Offset = 0.2
```

Verified: the modifier attaches, and its outputs and controls are as listed. Not verified: the output in a scratch comp reads None, because there's no Fairlight analysis. The clip name, media ID and analysis options need a clip in Resolve, so the values for a real clip are not checked here.

### Tips

- Set the analysis and clip in the Inspector, which lists the options, then script the scale and offset.
- Check the result in Resolve, since no value is available from a scratch comp.

**See also:** MIDI Extractor (`MIDI`), Resolve Parameter (`ResolveParameter`), Random (`KD_NumberRandom`).

## Follower (`StyledTextFollower`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** Follower · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to the StyledText input of a Text+) · **Output:** `StyledText` (Text)

Animates the characters of a Text+ one after another. You set up the animation on one character with the Follower's own controls, the same set of inputs as the Text+ Transform and Shading tabs, and the Follower applies it to the other characters with a timing set by Order and Delay. Attach it to the text of a Text+ (`StyledText`), not to a Text+ input such as Size. The Follower's output is text, which the Text+ then draws.

**Use for:** kinetic titles, per-character fades and slide-ins, typewriter-style reveals and any text where each letter moves on its own timing.

Keys go on the Follower's own inputs, not on the Text+. Number controls take a BezierSpline (for example `Opacity1`), and Point controls take a PolyPath (for example `CharacterOffset`), as on any tool. The Order and Delay settings decide when each character reaches the keyed value.

Modifiers are not added with AddTool. Attach the Follower with `AddModifier`, as shown in the example, and reach its controls through the Text+'s `StyledText` input.

### Timing tab

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Range | `Range` | Multi-button | 0: All Characters, 1: Character Range | Which characters the Follower affects. Character Range uses First and Last Character. |
| First Character | `FirstCharacter` | Number | 0 (0–50) | First character of a Character Range, counted from 0. |
| Last Character | `LastCharacter` | Number | 20 (0–50) | Last character of a Character Range. |
| Order | `Order` | Combo | 7: Automatic (0: Left to Right, 1: Right to Left, 2: Inside Out, 3: Outside In, 4: Random But One by One, 5: Completely Random, 6: Manual Curve) | The sequence in which the characters take the animation. Automatic is listed first in the Inspector, but its value is 7. |
| Delay Type | `DelayType` | Combo | 1 (0: None, 1: Between Each Character, 2: Between First and Last Character) | Whether a delay is added between characters, and over what span. |
| Delay | `Delay` | Number | 0 (−25 to 25) | The delay in frames between characters, as set by Delay Type. With Between Each Character and Delay 5, each character starts 5 frames after the one before it. |
| Delay by Character Position | `DelayByCharacterPosition` | Number | 0 (0–50) | Delay added according to each character's position in the text. |

### Animated inputs

The Follower's animatable controls are its Transform and Shading inputs. These are the Text+ inputs with the same names, copied onto the Follower. The examples use two of them:

| Control | ID | Type | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|
| Opacity (element 1) | `Opacity1` | Number | Opacity of shading element 1 (the fill). Keyed with a BezierSpline. |
| Character Offset | `CharacterOffset` | Point | Moves each character. Keyed with a PolyPath. |
| Character Offset Z | `CharacterOffsetZ` | Number | Moves each character in depth. |
| Character Size X, Y | `CharacterSizeX`, `CharacterSizeY` | Number | Scales each character (1 is normal). |
| Character Angle X, Y, Z | `CharacterAngleX`, `CharacterAngleY`, `CharacterAngleZ` | Number | Rotates each character, in degrees. |
| Character Spacing | `CharacterSpacing` | Number | Spacing between characters (1 is normal). |

Shading inputs for other elements follow the same pattern with numbers 2–8 (for example `Opacity2`). Their colours are `Red1`, `Green1`, `Blue1` and `Alpha1`.

### Example

A title that fades in and slides up, one character after another, from left to right.

```python
title = comp.AddTool('TextPlus')
title.StyledText = 'Hello world'
title.Size = 0.08
title.Center = [0.5, 0.5]

title.AddModifier('StyledText', 'StyledTextFollower')
fol = title.StyledText.GetConnectedOutput().GetTool()   # the Follower
fol.Order = 0                                           # Left to Right
fol.DelayType = 1                                       # Between Each Character
fol.Delay = 1                                           # delay per character

fol.Opacity1 = comp.BezierSpline()                      # fade in, frames 0-12
fol.Opacity1[0] = 0.0
fol.Opacity1[12] = 1.0

fol.CharacterOffset = comp.PolyPath()                   # slide up, frames 0-12
fol.CharacterOffset[0] = [0.0, -0.05]
fol.CharacterOffset[12] = [0.0, 0.0]
```

Verified: the Follower attaches to the text (`AddModifier` returns True), and every control in the example reads back as set. The Follower's `Opacity1` reads 0.0 at frame 0, 0.5 at frame 6 and 1.0 at frame 12, and `CharacterOffset` reads [0.0, −0.05] at frame 0 and [0.0, 0.0] at frame 12. The per-character timing (which character fades when) is not verified here: a scratch comp can't render or read the per-character result, so the timing has to be checked in the viewer.

### Tips

- Keyframe the Follower, not the Text+. Animating the Text+'s own Transform moves all the text together.
- Set Order and Delay before you judge the animation. The default Order is 7 (Automatic), so set Order explicitly if you
  want a fixed sequence.
- **How the timing works (verified by rendering).** Each character plays the Follower's keyed animation once, starting
  Delay frames after the previous character in the chosen Order. With `Opacity1` keyed 0 → 1 over frames 0–10, Delay Type
  Between Each Character and Delay 5, eight characters at frame 12 have these opacities, left to right:
  Left to Right (0) 1, 0.7, 0.2, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0; Right to Left (1) the reverse; Inside Out (2) 0, 0.2, 0.7, 1, 1, 0.7, 0.2, 0;
  Outside In (3) 1, 0.7, 0.2, 0, 0, 0.2, 0.7, 1. The Follower's text output is unchanged, so the result can only be
  seen in the rendered image.
- Use `Range` = 1 with `FirstCharacter` and `LastCharacter` to animate only part of the text.
- Enable and key a Shading element other than 1 (`Enabled2`, `Opacity2`) to add an outline or shadow that moves with the characters.
- Per-character styling (colour or size for chosen characters) is a different job: see Character Level Styling (`StyledTextCLS`).

**See also:** Text+ (`TextPlus`), Character Level Styling (`StyledTextCLS`), TextScramble (`TextScramble`), Transform (`Transform`).

## Formula (`KD_TextFormula`)

**Category:** Modifiers · **Short name:** Frm · **Inputs:** none (a modifier: connect it to a Text input). Its own inputs are the numbers `n1`–`n9`, points `p1`–`p9` and texts `t1`–`t9` · **Output:** `Output` (Text)

Writes numbers, points and text into a line of text. Type the line with placeholders, and the modifier replaces each one with the current value of the matching input: `n1` with the number n1, `p1x` and `p1y` with the two parts of point p1, and `t1` with the text t1. Numbers and points are formatted with their own precision, digits and spacing. Because the inputs are ordinary controls, they can be keyframed or linked to other tools.

**Use for:** live counters and readouts, coordinates in a caption, and text that shows the value of a control, such as a slider or a position, as it animates.

Modifiers are not added with AddTool. Attach one to a text input with `AddModifier`, as in the example, and reach its controls through that input.

| Control | ID | Type | Default / range | What it does |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Text | `Text` | Text | none | The line with placeholders. The output is this line, with each placeholder replaced. |
| Number inputs | `n1` … `n9` | Number | 0 (0–1) | Replaces `n1`…`n9` in the line. |
| Point inputs | `p1` … `p9` | Point | (0.5, 0.5) | Replaces `p1x`/`p1y` … `p9x`/`p9y` in the line, with the x and y values. |
| Text inputs | `t1` … `t9` | Text | none | Replaces `t1`…`t9` in the line. |
| Numbers Precision | `NumbersPrecision` | Number | 2 (0–6) | Decimal places for the `n` values. |
